concepts.definition: The real time between two measurements (in seconds). The angle integral, the filter and PID's derivative and integral terms depend on it.
concepts.example: Assuming dt = 0.005 while a round takes 5.35 ms makes the angle come out about 6.5% short.
concepts.pitfall: Writing dt as a constant without measuring whether the loop really runs at that time.

concepts.definition: delay(5) only waits 5 ms; the round's work is added on top, so the round gets longer by the work and changes.
concepts.example: If I2C reading and calculation take 0.35 ms, the round takes 5.35 ms.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking you have made a "200 Hz loop" with delay(5).

concepts.definition: Keeping the time of the next round and adding the period to it every round; small delays do not build up.
concepts.example: sonPlanUs += 5000; each round is planned 5000 µs apart.
concepts.pitfall: Writing sonPlanUs = simdi: each delay is added to the next one and the period drifts away from the target.

concepts.definition: When the work takes longer than one round, the round is missed. It is noticed with a counter, the plan is resynchronised and the real dt is still measured.
concepts.example: 12 ms of heavy work misses one round at a 5 ms period.
concepts.pitfall: Not keeping an overrun counter: missed rounds go unnoticed and the robot wobbles for no clear reason.

concepts.definition: micros() counts in 32 bits and wraps around after about 71.6 minutes. If the subtraction is done with unsigned long, the difference comes out right even across the wrap-around.
concepts.example: With simdi = 50 and sonUs = 4294967000, the unsigned difference is 346 µs.
concepts.pitfall: Taking the difference as an int: on AVR an int is 16 bits and overflows for differences longer than 32.7 ms.

quiz.prompt: There is a delay(5) at the end of a control loop. Which is true about the loop?
options: A round always takes exactly 5 ms
A round takes 5 ms plus the time of the work in the round, and can change every round
A round takes less than 5 ms, because delay speeds up the processor
delay(5) sets up an interrupt and runs every 5 ms
quiz.explanation: delay adds its waiting time to the round's work: the time for I2C reading, calculation and Serial.print comes on top of the 5 ms. So the round time is neither exactly 5 ms nor constant. In the simulation an average of 5.35 ms and a longest round of 6.64 ms were measured.

quiz.prompt: The gyroscope rotates at a constant 50 °/s for 4 seconds (real angle 200°). The loop really runs every 5.35 ms, but the code writes aci += hiz * 0.005. How many degrees does the code find?
quiz.explanation: The number of rounds is 4 / 0.00535 ≈ 747.7; each round adds 50·0.005 = 0.25°: 747.7·0.25 ≈ 186.9°. The ratio found is 5/5.35 = 93.5%, so about a 6.5% error. If the real dt had been measured, it would have come out as exactly 200°.

quiz.prompt: micros() counts microseconds in 32 bits (from 0 to 4 294 967 295). How many minutes after the board is switched on does it wrap around?
quiz.explanation: 2^32 µs = 4 294.97 seconds ≈ 71.6 minutes. If the subtraction is done with unsigned long, the difference between two measurements comes out right even at the moment of wrap-around; the only problem is taking the difference in a small type such as int.

options: Line 1: millis() should be used instead of micros()
Line 2: > should be written instead of <
Line 3: it should be sonPlanUs += PERIYOT_US; assigning simdi builds up the delays
Line 4: islemYap() should be called outside the loop
quiz.explanation: The loop may enter the work some time after the period has run out. Writing sonPlanUs = simdi adds this delay to the start of the next round and the period keeps getting longer. With +=, the planned moment moves forward in fixed steps and the delay does not build up. The comparison on line 2 is correct.

quiz.prompt:
This code runs just after micros() has wrapped around. What does it print?

```
unsigned long simdi = 50;             // sarmadan sonra
unsigned long sonUs = 4294967000UL;  // sarmadan önce
Serial.println(simdi - sonUs);
```
quiz.explanation: unsigned long is calculated modulo 2^32: 50 - 4294967000 = -4294966950, and adding 4294967296 to this gives 346. So there are 346 µs between two measurements taken 296 µs before and 50 µs after the wrap-around. No minus sign appears because the type is unsigned.
